{{Short description|Aspect of algebraic number theory}}
In [[mathematics]], the interplay between the [[Galois group]] ''G'' of a [[Galois extension]] ''L'' of a [[number field]] ''K'', and the way the [[prime ideal]]s ''P'' of the [[ring of integers]] ''O''<sub>''K''</sub> factorise as products of prime ideals of ''O''<sub>''L''</sub>, provides one of the richest parts of [[algebraic number theory]]. The '''splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions''' is sometimes attributed to [[David Hilbert]] by calling it '''Hilbert theory'''. There is a geometric analogue, for [[ramified covering]]s of [[Riemann surface]]s, which is simpler in that only one kind of subgroup of ''G'' need be considered, rather than two. This was certainly familiar before Hilbert.

== Definitions ==
Let ''L''/''K'' be a finite extension of number fields, and let ''O<sub>K</sub>'' and ''O<sub>L</sub>'' be the corresponding [[ring of integers]] of ''K'' and ''L'', respectively, which are defined to be the [[integral closure]] of the integers '''Z''' in the field in question.
: <math> \begin{array}{ccc} O_K & \hookrightarrow & O_L \\ \downarrow & & \downarrow \\ K & \hookrightarrow & L \end{array} </math>
Finally, let ''p'' be a non-zero prime ideal in ''O<sub>K</sub>'', or equivalently, a [[maximal ideal]], so that the residue ''O<sub>K</sub>''/''p'' is a [[field (mathematics)|field]].

From the basic theory of one-[[Krull dimension|dimensional]] rings follows the existence of a unique decomposition
: <math> pO_L = \prod_{j=1}^{g} P_j^{e_j} </math>

of the ideal ''pO<sub>L</sub>'' generated in ''O<sub>L</sub>'' by ''p'' into a product of distinct maximal ideals ''P''<sub>''j''</sub>, with multiplicities ''e''<sub>''j''</sub>.

The field ''F'' = ''O<sub>K</sub>''/''p'' naturally embeds into ''F''<sub>''j''</sub> = ''O<sub>L</sub>''/''P''<sub>''j''</sub> for every ''j'', the degree ''f''<sub>''j''</sub> = [''O<sub>L</sub>''/''P''<sub>''j''</sub> : ''O<sub>K</sub>''/''p''] of this '''residue field extension''' is called '''inertia degree''' of ''P''<sub>''j''</sub> over ''p''.

The multiplicity ''e''<sub>''j''</sub> is called '''ramification index''' of ''P''<sub>''j''</sub> over ''p''. If it is bigger than 1 for some ''j'', the field extension ''L''/''K'' is called '''ramified''' at ''p'' (or we say that ''p'' ramifies in ''L'', or that it is ramified in ''L''). Otherwise, ''L''/''K'' is called '''unramified''' at ''p''.  If this is the case then by the [[Chinese remainder theorem]] the quotient ''O<sub>L</sub>''/''pO<sub>L</sub>'' is a product of fields ''F''<sub>''j''</sub>. The extension ''L''/''K'' is ramified in exactly those primes that divide the [[Discriminant of an algebraic number field#Relative discriminant|relative discriminant]], hence the extension is unramified in all but finitely many prime ideals.

{{anchor|split prime|inert prime|ramified prime}}
Multiplicativity of [[ideal norm]] implies
: <math>[L:K]=\sum_{j=1}^{g} e_j f_j.</math>

If ''f''<sub>''j''</sub> = ''e''<sub>''j''</sub> = 1 for every ''j'' (and thus ''g'' = [''L'' : ''K'']), we say that ''p'' '''splits completely''' in ''L''. If ''g'' = 1 and ''f''<sub>''1''</sub> = 1 (and so ''e''<sub>''1''</sub> = [''L'' : ''K'']), we say that ''p'' '''ramifies completely''' in ''L''. Finally, if ''g'' = 1 and ''e''<sub>''1''</sub> = 1 (and so ''f''<sub>''1''</sub> = [''L'' : ''K'']), we say that ''p'' is '''inert''' in ''L''.

===The Galois situation===
In the following, the extension ''L''/''K'' is assumed to be a [[Galois extension]]. Then the [[prime avoidance lemma]] can be used to show the [[Galois group]] <math>G=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)</math> [[transitive group action|acts transitively]] on the ''P''<sub>''j''</sub>. That is, the prime ideal factors of ''p'' in ''L'' form a single [[orbit (group theory)|orbit]] under the [[automorphism]]s of ''L'' over ''K''. From this and the [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic|unique factorisation theorem]], it follows that ''f'' = ''f''<sub>''j''</sub> and ''e'' = ''e''<sub>''j''</sub> are independent of ''j''; something that certainly need not be the case for extensions that are not Galois. The basic relations then read
: <math>pO_L = \left(\prod_{j=1}^{g} P_j\right)^e</math>.
and
: <math>[L:K]=efg.</math>
The relation above shows that [''L'' : ''K'']/''ef'' equals the number ''g'' of prime factors of ''p'' in ''O<sub>L</sub>''. By the [[orbit-stabilizer formula]] this number is also equal to {{math|{{mabs|''G''}}/{{mabs|''D''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>}}}} for every ''j'', where ''D''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>, the '''decomposition group''' of ''P''<sub>''j''</sub>, is the subgroup of elements of ''G'' sending a given ''P''<sub>''j''</sub> to itself. Since the degree of ''L''/''K'' and the order of ''G'' are equal by basic Galois theory, it follows that the order of the decomposition group ''D''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub> is  ''ef'' for every ''j''.

This decomposition group contains a subgroup {{math|''I''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>}}, called '''inertia group''' of ''P''<sub>''j''</sub>, consisting of automorphisms of ''L''/''K'' that induce the identity automorphism on ''F''<sub>''j''</sub>. In other words, {{math|''I''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>}} is the kernel of reduction map <math>D_{P_j}\to\operatorname{Gal}(F_j/F)</math>. It can be shown that this map is surjective, and it follows that <math>\operatorname{Gal}(F_j/F)</math> is isomorphic to {{math|''D''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>/''I''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>}} and the order of the inertia group {{math|''I''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>}} is ''e''.

The theory of the [[Frobenius element]] goes further, to identify an element of {{math|''D''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub> / ''I''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>}} for given ''j'' which corresponds to the Frobenius automorphism in the Galois group of the finite field extension ''F''<sub>''j''</sub> / ''F''. In the unramified case the order of ''D''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub> is ''f'' and {{math|''I''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>}} is trivial, so the Frobenius element is in this case an element of ''D''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub>, and thus also an element of ''G''. For varying ''j'', the groups ''D''<sub>''P''<sub>''j''</sub></sub> are conjugate subgroups inside ''G'': Recalling that ''G'' acts transitively on the ''P''<sub>''j''</sub>, one checks that if {{mvar|&sigma;}} maps ''P''<sub>''j''</sub> to ''P''<sub>{{prime|''j''}}</sub>, <math>\sigma D_{P_j} \sigma^{-1} = D_{P_{j'}}</math>. Therefore, if ''G'' is an [[abelian group]], the Frobenius element of an unramified prime ''P'' does not depend on which ''P''<sub>''j''</sub> we take. Furthermore, in the abelian case, associating an unramified prime of ''K'' to its Frobenius and extending multiplicatively defines a homomorphism from the group of unramified ideals of ''K'' into ''G''. This map, known as the '''Artin map''', is a crucial ingredient of [[class field theory]], which studies the finite abelian extensions of a given number field ''K''.<ref>Milne, J.S. (2020). [https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf Class Field Theory.]</ref>

In the geometric analogue, for [[complex manifold]]s or [[algebraic geometry]] over an [[algebraically closed field]], the concepts of ''decomposition group'' and ''inertia group'' coincide. There, given a Galois ramified cover, all but finitely many points have the same number of [[preimage]]s.

The splitting of primes in extensions that are not Galois may be studied by using a [[splitting field]] initially, i.e. a Galois extension that is somewhat larger. For example, [[cubic field]]s usually are 'regulated' by a degree 6 field containing them.

== Example — the Gaussian integers ==

This section describes the splitting of prime ideals in the field extension '''Q'''({{itco|''i''}})/'''Q'''. That is, we take ''K'' = '''Q''' and ''L'' = '''Q'''({{itco|''i''}}), so ''O''<sub>''K''</sub> is simply '''Z''', and ''O''<sub>''L''</sub> = '''Z'''[{{itco|''i''}}] is the ring of [[Gaussian integers]]. Although this case is far from representative — after all, '''Z'''[{{itco|''i''}}] has [[unique factorisation]], and [[Heegner number|there aren't many imaginary quadratic fields with unique factorization]] — it exhibits many of the features of the theory.

Writing ''G'' for the Galois group of '''Q'''({{itco|''i''}})/'''Q''', and σ for the complex conjugation automorphism in ''G'', there are three cases to consider.

=== The prime ''p'' = 2 ===

The prime 2 of '''Z''' ramifies in '''Z'''[{{itco|''i''}}]:
:<math>(2)=(1+i)^2</math>
The ramification index here is therefore ''e'' = 2. The residue field is
:<math>O_L / (1+i)O_L</math>
which is the finite field with two elements. The decomposition group must be equal to all of ''G'', since there is only one prime of '''Z'''[{{itco|''i''}}] above 2. The inertia group is also all of ''G'', since
:<math>a+bi\equiv a-bi\bmod1+i</math>
for any integers ''a'' and ''b'', as <math>a+bi = 2bi + a-bi =(1+i) \cdot (1-i)bi + a-bi \equiv a-bi \bmod 1+i</math> .

In fact, 2 is the ''only'' prime that ramifies in '''Z'''[{{itco|''i''}}], since every prime that ramifies must divide the [[discriminant of an algebraic number field|discriminant]] of '''Z'''[{{itco|''i''}}], which is &minus;4.

=== Primes ''p'' &equiv; 1 mod 4 ===

Any prime ''p'' ≡ 1 mod 4 ''splits'' into two distinct prime ideals in '''Z'''[{{itco|''i''}}]; this is a manifestation of [[Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares]]. For example:
:<math>13=(2+3i)(2-3i)</math>
The decomposition groups in this case are both the [[trivial group]] {1}; indeed the automorphism σ ''switches'' the two primes ({{itco|2 + 3''i''}}) and ({{itco|2 &minus; 3''i''}}), so it cannot be in the decomposition group of either prime. The inertia group, being a subgroup of the decomposition group, is also the trivial group. There are two residue fields, one for each prime,
:<math>O_L / (2 \pm 3i)O_L\ ,</math>
which are both isomorphic to the finite field with 13 elements. The Frobenius element is the trivial automorphism; this means that
:<math>(a+bi)^{13}\equiv a + bi\bmod2\pm3i</math>
for any integers ''a'' and ''b''.

=== Primes ''p'' &equiv; 3 mod 4 ===

Any prime ''p'' ≡ 3 mod 4 remains ''inert'' in '''Z'''[{{itco|''i''}}]; that is, it does ''not'' split. For example, (7) remains prime in '''Z'''[{{itco|''i''}}]. In this situation, the decomposition group is all of ''G'', again because there is only one prime factor. However, this situation differs from the ''p'' = 2 case, because now σ does ''not'' act trivially on the residue field
:<math>O_L / (7)O_L\ ,</math>
which is the finite field with 7<sup>2</sup> = 49 elements. For example, the difference between <math>1+i</math> and <math>\sigma(1 + i) = 1 - i</math> is <math>2i</math>, which is certainly not divisible by 7. Therefore, the inertia group is the trivial group {1}. The Galois group of this residue field over the subfield '''Z'''/7'''Z''' has order 2, and is generated by the image of the Frobenius element. The Frobenius element is none other than σ; this means that
:<math>(a+bi)^7\equiv a-bi\bmod7</math>
for any integers ''a'' and ''b''.

== Computing the factorisation ==

Suppose that we wish to determine the factorisation of a prime ideal ''P'' of ''O''<sub>''K''</sub> into primes of ''O''<sub>''L''</sub>. The following procedure (Neukirch, p.&nbsp;47) solves this problem in many cases. The strategy is to select an integer θ in ''O''<sub>''L''</sub> so that ''L'' is generated over ''K'' by θ (such a θ is guaranteed to exist by the [[primitive element theorem]]), and then to examine the [[Minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] ''H''(''X'') of θ over ''K''; it is a [[monic polynomial]] with coefficients in ''O''<sub>''K''</sub>. Reducing the coefficients of ''H''(''X'') modulo ''P'', we obtain a monic polynomial ''h''(''X'') with coefficients in ''F'', the (finite) residue field ''O''<sub>''K''</sub>/''P''. Suppose that ''h''(''X'') factorises in the polynomial ring ''F''[''X''] as
: <math> h(X) = h_1(X)^{e_1} \cdots h_n(X)^{e_n}, </math>
where the ''h''<sub>''j''</sub> are distinct monic irreducible polynomials in ''F''[''X'']. Then, as long as ''P'' is not one of finitely many exceptional primes (the precise condition is described below), the factorisation of ''P'' has the following form:
: <math> P O_L = Q_1^{e_1} \cdots Q_n^{e_n}, </math>
where the ''Q''<sub>''j''</sub> are distinct prime ideals of ''O''<sub>''L''</sub>. Furthermore, the inertia degree of each ''Q''<sub>''j''</sub> is equal to the degree of the corresponding polynomial ''h''<sub>''j''</sub>, and there is an explicit formula for the ''Q''<sub>''j''</sub>:
: <math> Q_j = P O_L + h_j(\theta) O_L, </math>
where ''h''<sub>''j''</sub> denotes here a lifting of the polynomial ''h''<sub>''j''</sub> to ''K''[''X''].
   
In the Galois case, the inertia degrees are all equal, and the ramification indices ''e''<sub>1</sub> = ... = ''e''<sub>''n''</sub> are all equal.

The exceptional primes, for which the above result does not necessarily hold, are the ones not relatively prime to the [[conductor (ring theory)|conductor]] of the ring ''O''<sub>''K''</sub>[θ]. The conductor is defined to be the ideal
: <math> \{ y \in O_L : yO_L \subseteq O_K[\theta]\}; </math>
it measures how far the [[order (ring theory)|order]] ''O''<sub>''K''</sub>[θ] is from being the whole ring of integers (maximal order) ''O''<sub>''L''</sub>.

A significant caveat is that there exist examples of ''L''/''K'' and ''P'' such that there is ''no'' available θ that satisfies the above hypotheses (see for example <ref>{{cite book |first=William A. |last=Stein |chapter=Essential Discriminant Divisors |chapter-url=https://www.wstein.org/papers/undergrad/decomp/decomp/node4.html |title=Factoring Primes in Rings of Integers |date=2002 |url=https://www.wstein.org/papers/undergrad/decomp/decomp/}}</ref>). Therefore, the algorithm given above cannot be used to factor such ''P'', and more sophisticated approaches must be used, such as that described in.<ref>{{harvnb|Stein|2002|loc=[https://www.wstein.org/papers/undergrad/decomp/decomp/node3.html Method that Always Works]}}</ref>

=== An example ===

Consider again the case of the Gaussian integers. We take θ to be the imaginary unit <math>i</math>, with minimal polynomial ''H''(''X'') = ''X''<sup>2</sup> + 1. Since '''Z'''[<math>i</math>] is the whole ring of integers of '''Q'''(<math>i</math>), the [[Conductor (class field theory)|conductor]] is the unit ideal, so there are no exceptional primes.

For ''P'' = (2), we need to work in the field '''Z'''/(2)'''Z''', which amounts to factorising the polynomial ''X''<sup>2</sup> + 1 modulo 2:
: <math>X^2 + 1 = (X+1)^2 \pmod 2.</math>
Therefore, there is only one prime factor, with inertia degree 1 and ramification index 2, and it is given by
: <math>Q = (2)\mathbf Z[i] + (i+1)\mathbf Z[i] = (1+i)\mathbf Z[i].</math>

The next case is for ''P'' = (''p'') for a prime ''p'' ≡ 3 mod 4. For concreteness we will take ''P'' = (7). The polynomial ''X''<sup>2</sup> + 1 is irreducible modulo 7. Therefore, there is only one prime factor, with inertia degree 2 and ramification index 1, and it is given by
: <math>Q = (7)\mathbf Z[i] + (i^2 + 1)\mathbf Z[i] = 7\mathbf Z[i].</math>

The last case is ''P'' = (''p'') for a prime ''p'' ≡ 1 mod 4; we will again take ''P'' = (13). This time we have the factorisation
: <math>X^2 + 1 = (X + 5)(X - 5) \pmod{13}.</math>
Therefore, there are ''two'' prime factors, both with inertia degree and ramification index 1. They are given by
: <math>Q_1 = (13)\mathbf Z[i] + (i + 5)\mathbf Z[i] = \cdots = (2+3i)\mathbf Z[i]</math>
and
: <math>Q_2 = (13)\mathbf Z[i] + (i - 5)\mathbf Z[i] = \cdots = (2-3i)\mathbf Z[i].</math>
